title: Arjuna's shaking hands
hook: the finest archer in the army can't hold his bow, and Krishna's answer reaches down to the breath
carry: samatva: evenness in success and failure is yoga

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachiketa at Death's door, and Yama's chariot: atman is the rider, not the horses.

Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra, conch shells blaring. Arjuna, the finest archer on either side, asks his charioteer, Krishna, to drive him out between them so he can see who he's fighting. He sees teachers. Uncles. Cousins. And his body gives out. His limbs go weak, his mouth goes dry, his skin burns, his hair stands on end, and his great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. He can't stand. He sits down in the chariot.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, CONCHES BLARING.` → `HE SEES HIS OWN FAMILY.` → `THE BOW SLIPS FROM HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: That's how the Bhagavad Gita begins: not with a calm sage, but with a body in panic. Yesterday's picture comes alive here: a chariot, a driver, and a rider who has forgotten who he is. Krishna's teaching meets him there. In the second chapter he gives it a name. Your right is to the action, never to its fruits. So do the work, without clinging, the same in success and in failure. Evenness, samatva, is called yoga. It runs through the whole Gita: even in pleasure and pain, even toward friend and foe. And it reaches all the way down to the body. In the fifth chapter, Krishna describes the sage at practice: the outside world shut out, the gaze resting between the brows, the in-breath and the out-breath made even as they move within the nostrils, free of desire, fear and anger. Many teachers read the two passages together: Arjuna's body shook because his mind was torn over what the battle would cost, and Krishna's answer is an even mind, with an even breath traveling with it. This is the heart of what Hindus call karma yoga: you do your dharma, your rightful work, fully, and you offer the result instead of clutching it. If everything hangs on the result, the hands shake. If the result is offered, the breath can settle. So the breath practice of these days ends here: the breath honored as prana, the rider in the chariot, and now in and out made even, because the one breathing has let go of the outcome.
screen: `THE ACTION IS YOURS, NOT THE FRUIT.` · `SAMATVA: EVENNESS IS YOGA.` · `IN-BREATH AND OUT-BREATH MADE EVEN.` · `KARMA YOGA: DO THE WORK, OFFER THE RESULT.`

segments.voice: With place and body settled, let the breath swing a little for a few rounds, a slightly longer out-breath, then a slightly longer in-breath. Then let them meet, in for four and out for four, quiet within the nostrils. When it's steady, bring to mind one thing waiting for you today, and offer how it turns out, in a prayer if you pray, or just by loosening your grip on it; then see if the breath stays level on its own.
Pranayama sequences. Breath practices set in an order. Today, where the Gita lets them rest: in-breath and out-breath made even, an even breath for an even mind.
Hold on to it: samatva, evenness in success and failure is yoga. Arjuna's bow slipped, and Krishna began right there. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindus who practice pranayama close with a few rounds of even breathing, a practice teachers connect with Gita 5.27; many also offer the result of their work to God, the karma yoga of Gita 2.47–2.48.
